utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I have, I think, a relatively brief summary to read. It shouldn't take more than five to seven minutes, I think, to get through. And then I just have a few questions in relation to these exhibits. Thank you, Mr. President. The witness is a survivor of the mass execution in Orahovac of over 1.000 Muslim men and boys on 14 July 1995. On 11 July 1995, the witness lived with his family in a hamlet in Srebrenica. At around 5.00 p.m., the witness saw a column of villagers who called out to him, saying that Srebrenica had fallen. The witness immediately went home to find his neighbours with packed bags, who told the witness that a civilian protection official had told them that the old and infirm should go to the UNPROFOR base in Potocari, while military-age men should try to save themselves by going through the forest. The witness cobbled together a few belongings and with his wife and family set off for the UNPROFOR base. They joined a column of neighbouring villagers travelling on foot some three hours to Potocari. The witness travelled on horseback because of an old injury to his leg which made it difficult for him to walk. Upon reaching Potocari after nightfall, the witness, like many others, spent the night with his family in the parking lot of the Sacmara factory near the UNPROFOR compound. On the morning of 12 July, the witness heard the transportation to Tuzla had been organised. As he waited, the witness saw Serb soldiers coming toward the factories near the UNPROFOR base. They set fire to the haystacks as they approached. At about 2.00 p.m., the first convoys arrived. The witness went to the main road where he saw barricades. On the narrowing roadway leading to the waiting buses and trucks, the witness saw UNPROFOR soldiers lined up. Further down, the witness saw Serb soldiers who were lined up near the buses and trucks, close to a battery factory. As the witness approached the buses, Serb soldiers separated him from his family. He was taken aside and ordered to join the other elderly men at the other end of the road who had already been singled out. The witness saw other men continuing to be separated from their families as he was detained with approximately 20 other elderly men and guarded by five or six Serb soldiers. The men were taken to an unfinished house near the main road. As they arrived, they were threatened by some of the soldiers and forced to sit on the ground. Group after group of prisoners arrived, eventually filling up the room where the witness was held. Thereafter, arriving prisoners were forced to sit outside in front of the full building. All of the prisoners taken to the house were elderly and disabled. During the four hours they were at the house, the prisoners were provided with no food or water. As it became dark, the men were taken to two buses which were filled to capacity. They were driven to Bratunac and met there by 10 to 15 Serb soldiers in front of what appeared to the witness to be an abandoned warehouse near the Vuk Karadzic school. The prisoners were taken inside and made to sit down as soldiers guarded the entrance. The witness recalled that the warehouse had no real floor, with only planks with sand in between them on the ground. Men continued to be brought into the warehouse until around midnight, when it finally became full. The witness estimated that about 400 prisoners were held there. The prisoners were kept in stifling heat and overcrowded conditions, without food or water. Their complaints were answered only with threats and violence. Throughout the night of the 12 July, Serb soldiers took out about 40 prisoners from the warehouse, and the witness could hear blunt blows being struck, moaning and screaming. Some men returned to the room, were bloodied, and died overnight. The witness recalled one prisoners being taken out of the room. He heard shots and then soldiers saying, "You can drag him away. He's finished. He's dead." On the morning of 13 July, the prisoners were allowed to remove the dead among them from the warehouse. Those who did described a pile of bodies that they saw behind the warehouse when they returned. The witness also recalled seeing a man severely beaten by a soldier that morning. That prisoner was struck by one soldier first with an iron bar and then by another with an axe. Later, Serb soldiers demanded that the prisoners surrender their valuables and other property, including their identifications. The soldiers resumed calling prisoners out of the warehouse and killing them. The witness estimated that throughout the day another 40 men were killed. That evening, the witness recalled that General Mladic arrived at the warehouse. He told the prisoners that they would be taken to Kalesija for exchange. At that time, 296 prisoners were counted. Soon after, six buses arrived which the men were forced to board. Each bus was secured by a Serb soldier with an automatic rifle. The convoy of buses set out from Bratunac at around 8.00 or 9.00 p.m. on the evening of 14 July, stopping at Drinjaca on the way. En route, the buses proceeded north past Zvornik toward Karakaj and then west to the Grbavci school in Orahovac. The witness estimated that the prisoners arrived at the school around 2.00 a.m. on the morning of 14 July. There they were met by 10 to 15 Serb soldiers, off-loaded, and taken inside the school's gym. The witness recalled that no food or water was provided, and as more and more prisoners filled the gym, the conditions deteriorated. One prisoner who complained about the conditions was taken out by a soldier. The witness then heard shots, and the prisoner never returned. According to the witness's recollection, the last of the prisoners arrived sometime around 10.00 a.m. on the morning of 14 July. The witness estimated that by that time roughly 2.500 prisoners were at the school. The witness recalled that General Mladic arrived at the school, telling the prisoners that some of them would be taken to Fikret Abdic and others to Bijeljina. Later the prisoners were blindfolded, led out of the gym and loaded onto a small TAM truck which travelled back and forth between the school and the nearby execution site. The witness recalled that when his turn came, he was placed aboard the truck, which proceeded along the road for a short distance before turning off into a pasture. The witness saw many bodies as the truck continued further to where he could see another group of bodies. There the struck stopped, and two soldiers opened the back. The men were taken off, told where to stand, and to keep quiet. As soon as the truck left the soldiers opened fire. The witness fell to the ground as other prisoners fell on and around him. As he lay still, the witness saw the TAM truck return with another group of prisoners. They were taken off, lined up in four rows, and then shot. The witness saw this happen repeatedly and into nightfall when prisoners continued to be executed under the lights of excavators brought to the site to dig their graves. The witness continued to lie still until the last TAM truck came and left, and everyone from the gym, it seemed, had been killed. Thereafter, the witness called out to see if any other prisoners had survived. Only one person responded, and together they made their escape. In the morning, they were joined by another survivor. The three arrived in the free territory on or about 19 July 1995. Your Honours, that concludes my summary. I have a few additional questions that I'd like to put to the witness at this time. May I proceed, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: PW-023

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE

utterances.text: And do you know what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: He was taken out, and he was mowed down by a -- with an automatic rifle. He was the only one who was shot dead with an automatic rifle that evening. All the others were killed by blunt blows.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me ask you about Gabeljic, Ibrahim. Do you know that name?

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.text: And how do you recognise this name?

utterances.text: Well, I knew him from before, but also we were together in Bratunac and at Potocarska Rijeka, so both in Potocarska Rijeka and in Bratunac we were together.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What about Gabeljic, Ibro? Do you recognise that name?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And do you know what happened to them?

utterances.text: I don't know. I can't really tell you whether they were killed in Bratunac or whether they got off at Orahovo, Grbavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And Hadzovic, Azem?

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: Azem Hadzovic, yes. I knew him, too, both from before, and I also saw him down there. He went to Orahovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: PW-023

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Muminovic, Hamed. Do you recognise that name?

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: I do. I know him too. He, too, went to Orahovo. He wasn't killed in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Hodzic, Huso.

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: I know Huso Hodzic too. Now, I don't know about him or where he was killed. I know that I saw him in Potocari and in Bratunac, but whether he stayed in Bratunac throughout this time or whether he was killed in Orahovo, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And Mustafic, Rahman.

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: Rahman Mustafic was with me also. I know him too. He arrived in Orahovo alive on the buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And do you know what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: Well, he never came back, so most probably he was executed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And Mustafic, Meho.

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: I know him too. He, too, was in Orahovo, and he didn't come back. So he was executed in Orahovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mujic, Aziz?

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: Aziz Mujic, too, was with me in Bratunac, but I don't know about how far he actually got after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Suljic, Nazif?

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: I know him too. He, too, reached Orahovo. He wasn't killed in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Hodzic, Zulfo.

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: Zulfo Hodzic was in Bratunac, but I do not know how far he got, whether he remained in Bratunac or got off in Orahovo. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Hasanovic, Hasib?

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: Hasib Hasanovic got off in Orahovo together with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Tursunovic, Adil.

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: Adil Tursunovic also got off with me at Orahovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mehmedovic, Izet?

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: Izet Mehmedovic, too, got off the vehicle together with me in Orahovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Gabeljic, Sevko?

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: Sevko Gabeljic, too, was with me when we got off the vehicle in Orahovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mekanic, Jakub?

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: Jakub Mekanic also got off the vehicle with me in Orahovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Ejubovic, Suljo?

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: Suljo Ejubovic also got to Orahovo with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If you could just tell us briefly what you remember about the building in Bratunac that you were taken to. If you could just describe it for the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: You mean the building we were taken to?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: We were taken to an abandoned agricultural warehouse, produce warehouse, and we were made to enter this warehouse. There was no light inside. The walls were painted white, but as this was an abandoned facility, there were no floors. There were just the beams between where the floor boards should be and then filled with sand. The holes were filled with sand. Now, below the ceiling there were some windows, but not on the right- or left-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And can you describe the entrance door.

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: The entrance door was larger than the regular doors, but there were no doors.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Well, thank you, Witness. I don't have any further questions for you at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Witness, you know that now the -- the accused has the right to put some questions to you. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, do you have questions for the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you, Your Honour. Can you hear me now? Thank you, Mr. President. I wish to bless everyone present in the courtroom and everyone who is listening or watching this trial. I also wish to greet Mr. Witness. I would have several questions for the witness, and I will address you as mister.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, you have given a statement 0079-8631 to this International Tribunal on the 2nd of April. The number is 1D41.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters could not hear the year of the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are on page 1 now. Could we please move on to the second page. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you see your statement?

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: I can see it, but I cannot not read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: All right. I will read to you. I will be reading from one line 1 to line 7. You were born in Srebrenica: "This is where I lived and worked. The situation in the town became critical on the 11th of July. Around 16 hours a soldier came and asked all the able men to come to the front line. I did not go because I'm an invalid and would not be able to fight. In 1982 I had an accident, and my leg was badly injured. Between 18 and 1900 hours, another soldier came and said that the line was falling and that all the able-bodied men should try to save themselves and that the rest of the population should go to the UNPROFOR base in Potocari." Thank you. Do you remember that you stated this in the statement which you gave?

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: I did not see either of these because I was in the field, but when I came back home, they told me that such and such a person had come, and they had been soldiers before demilitarisation. After the demilitarisation of Srebrenica, it was not a soldier anywhere. No one was wearing uniforms anyway. And someone who was not able bodied could not come to see persons such as me. He had to be more able bodied than myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you just answer whether this was correct, whether I read out to you as the statement says? Does it say that or not?

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: It's possible that that's what's in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Will you tell me who told you that a soldier had come to inform you that?

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: He did not say that the soldier had come, but it's possible. They asked me in Tuzla, Was he an able bodied man who came to inform you? And I said, Well, if he hadn't been able bodied, he wouldn't have able to walk. He wouldn't have been able to reach us. He had to be able bodied if he could walk from one village to another to tell us to go to the UNPROFOR base.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Will you just tell us if this was an official? Was it an official person?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I have to stop you. First Mr. Vanderpuye has the floor, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry, I didn't want to interrupt here. I just want to make sure we're not broadcasting this document; that's number one. And number 2, I want to make sure that we've identified correctly the date of the document for the record because I think the date that was indicated was 2nd April, which I don't believe is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We see on the screen another date, the 7th of July, 1996. Was it this document that you were asking for, Mr. Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The date of the interview was the 10th of August, 1995. Until the 12th of August, 1995. This is what the statement that was submitted to the Defence by the Prosecution says. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Is that the document on the screen? If you can be -- Mr. Vanderpuye, [indiscernible] it's -- it's not shown to the public.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes. This is not the correct document that's on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No. No. We should wait for the right document coming up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We will wait for the right document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Perhaps you can indicate the right number of the document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. President, the correct number of the document is 1D421. Thank you. This is what I said earlier when I mentioned the document and when I quoted from it. Mr. President, may I continue with the questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think we now have the right document on the screen, but not in the English yet. Please carry on, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I think that you can see it in English now and that it is visible from the document as I quoted that the witness said that the population was informed by a soldier that the able-bodied men should try to get away and that those who were considered civilians and were not able bodied should go to the UNPROFOR base in Potocari. The witness confirmed that he had mentioned that in his statement. Thank you. My question for the witness is the following:

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Was it the general practice even before that, that the population be informed through officials who would come in uniform or not in uniform to inform them about something that the authorities would have to tell them?

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: No, not until that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So on that day someone came who provided official information that Srebrenica had fallen and that the able-bodied men should try to save themselves and that those who are to be considered civilians should go to Potocari. Did I understand that properly are?

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So in your view, who could have given this information to the person who had come and passed on the information to you and other villagers?

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: What person?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Which institution?

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: I don't know I heard it from the villagers when I got home. I had no time to ask who had come to the village, what kind of a person that was or anything. They asked me in Tuzla, Was he an able-bodied man? Was it a man or a woman? I said, It was a man. This is what I was told. They asked, Was he an able-bodied man? I said, Of course he was. This is why maybe they described him as a soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm only interested in whether on the basis of this you could understand that this was an information that really originated from those who were responsible for everything and that it was not just hearsay.

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: Of course, because it was the truth. The entire day we were under artillery fire. No one could go anywhere out from a shelter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And what did your wife tell you when you got home?

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: She was with me in the field as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: What did your son and your daughter tell you?

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: That we should leave. There was nothing to talk about. Everything was packed. All the neighbours were waiting for us. They had packed their things, and they were waiting there in one place.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So everyone took this information as being true.

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Will you tell -- tell me, did you work normally with your family in the field?

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you tell me if anyone stayed in your village?

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: Yes. Just one man stayed there, but he was unable to move at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you know by any chance what happened with him later on?

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: I heard from his wife that they took him to Derventa and that they killed him in Derventa and that one man was saying that he knew where he was buried. I heard it from his wife and not from anyone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So you do not have any certain information?

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell me, did the villagers of other villages do the same, and did they receive the information that Srebrenica had fallen in the same manner and that the able-bodied men should try to escape, whereas the civilian population should move to the base in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: Most probably, yes. While we were passing through the villages, they had already been abandoned. There was no one there that night.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So you are sure that the information did not come from the army of the Republic of Serbia or another propaganda source but from the centre that was responsible to inform you?

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And who's responsibility was it to inform the civilian population and the able-bodied men in Srebrenica about such matters, can you tell us that? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: If anyone, then it was the president of the municipality, but I do not know who was responsible for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you tell us who was responsible of the military authorities.

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't tell you that because Naser was not there, and I did not know who took over his function and his obligations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Probably his deputy, because there's always a deputy in the army.

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: But there is always a deputy in the army. Do you know if that was so?

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: Well, of course there was one, but I wouldn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So you concluded that the information was carried on by the civilian and military authorities.

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: Well, somebody did pass them on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you are too fast again. You should pause before you put the next question to the witness. The interpreters are not able to follow that if you have this kind of speed.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, can you tell me whether on the road and upon leaving your village did you see the Serb army before you reached Potocari?

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you tell me how far your village was from Potocari?

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: Well, it's about 3 hours on foot across the hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell me whether other people who had come to Potocari with you told you that they had seen Serbian Army in their villages and on the roads along which they came to Potocari?

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: No, did I not hear that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell me whether you saw Serbian Army when you got to Potocari and when did you reach Potocari in the first place?

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: I reached Potocari during the night. I did not see anyone because it was dark. There were no lights. It was a moonlit night, but I could only see the civilians, that they had come there. I spent the night there, and in the morning I saw UNPROFOR, and I saw personnel carriers on the road, but they were quite far away from us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you just tell us for the sake of the transcript if it was on the day when the NATO aircraft targeted Serbian positions or if it was on another day because you never mentioned any date.

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: It was a different day. On the day when the NATO aircraft attacked, that was the night when we left off to go to Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you tell us what date that was?

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: It was the 11th.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And on the 12th?

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: On the 12th we left Potocari for Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So you believe that Srebrenica would not fall until you were informed by this official courier. Let me him call him that way. Whether he was a soldier or civilian, it doesn't matter. You thought that Srebrenica had not fallen, and you were working in the field as usual?

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So after 1700 hours when you were informed that Srebrenica had fallen and passed on the information that you should go to Potocari and that the able-bodied men should escape, that was what you did.

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Will you please also tell us, when did your son decide to go together with the able-bodied men who tried to get away and save themselves?

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: I never saw my son there. He was not home.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: All right. So he acted immediately in accordance with the information.

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. What do you think? Who sent the information that was relevant for him?

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't ask him today. I never asked him who did he hear that from.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. But you suppose that it was a courier who passed on the other information as well?

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Will you just please tell me whether your entire family left Srebrenica and reached Tuzla and the territory where the BH Army was situated.

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Will you tell me when was the first time you saw Serbian soldiers.

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: In Potocari. In Potocari, around the middle of the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So it was on the 12th around the middle of the day that you saw them first?

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: Yes, that was about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was there any shooting or killing until that time?

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: I didn't see any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Will you tell me whether there was any Serbian Army in the villages before that time and did they collect population around the villages, or did the villagers come to Potocari on their own?

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: In -- from the village that I passed through, the population had come on their own to Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us as an eyewitness whether the Serbian Army did anything in Srebrenica before the 12th when you saw it in Potocari against the civilians? Did they call on them to leave? Did they expel them from the villages, or did you come to Potocari because the courier told you to do so?

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: We did because the courier informed us about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us whether UNPROFOR knew that you were coming to their base in Potocari, and did they receive you in accordance with an earlier agreement?

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Will you tell me whether at the base in Potocari you heard that on the night between the 11th and the 12th General Mladic declared a unilateral cease-fire?

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Will you tell me if you heard in Potocari from anyone else whether there were any negotiations between the civilians and General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: Did I not hear that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Will you tell me if you heard anything about that while you were in the village and working in the field?

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: Hear what?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you hear anything about the negotiations between the civilian authorities and the army?

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: No, I didn't hear anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Witness. Will you please tell me when it was -- when was it your turn to board a bus and leave Potocari for Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: From Potocari to Bratunac first?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: When you thought you were going to Tuzla before you were separated. This is what I ask you. When did you board on a bus with your family?

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: When you -- when I started with my family, it could have been around 4.00. I'm not certain, but it was perhaps around 4.00. 4.00 p.m., I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: Immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: How many people were with you who were separated from the group of people who had come to Potocari?

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: How many people were separated?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Yes, roughly. Could you give us a number?

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: I know the number that was at the warehouse. There were around 400 men. They were separated on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Are you certain that 400 were separated on that day?

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: Well, I suppose, unless there were more. Around 40 were killed during the night, and then 10 were to be boarded on the next day. They left, and they never returned. That's around 50. And there were around 50 during the day. That's 100. And 296, you can calculate yourself how many that was. That's almost exactly -- if there were not more.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm asking you in the night between the 11th and 12th, how many people were separated in the bus and separated from their families? Can you tell us that?

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: I'm telling you what I saw, how many people were with me. This is what I saw. Whether any were separated anywhere else, I couldn't tell.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: All right. So you believe that all of them, all 400 were separated on the first day.

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: They came to Bratunac, all of them, and nobody came later on. That was certainly the number, and there could have been more.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. So you say that was on the 11th until the 12th in the evening. Please tell me now, did any of the women, children, and others who fell in the category of civilians were kept or brought to where you were?

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: One child came together with us. His grandfather brought him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So his grandfather brought him. What did they do with him? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: The child was crying, said he wanted to drink water. So they took him. They brought him out, and what did they do with him, I don't know, but the child did not come back.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So the child was there because the grandfather brought him.

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: Well, they asked him, "Why did you take the child with you?" And he said both his father and mother were killed and the child is alive. There was nobody else he could go with except myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: But the father and mother were not killed on that day?

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: No. It was maybe a month ago when the village was shelled. They were standing in front of the house, and it happened that they got killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So it was not with you at the gym in Bratunac. There were no women or children.

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: No. This was the only child that was there in the evening, and then no women or children after that point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Can you tell me whether you were younger than 60 or 55 at the time?

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: I was about 55 at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell me, you said in the statement you were not able bodied because of your previous injury. Did they consider you as an able-bodied man because of your age?

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: No, there were people who could not use either of their arms or who were born without arms or without one of the arms, and they were also together with me. There were four who were mute and deaf. They couldn't speak. All the four of them, I know their names and where they're from. All four of them were together with me, and they came to Orahovo together with me in the same bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm only asking you because you were an eyewitness, and you were actually separated as -- and declared able bodied because of your age and not because of your disability or ability.

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: Well, they took out people who were 70 years old or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: No. I'm asking about you.

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: Well, I don't know why it was. They would just say, You come this way, and you go that way. So I had to follow him. He didn't explain either why or what for they were they were separating us. They would just tell us, You are going this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, tell me, did you ever discuss with your son later on how he managed to flee and to save himself?

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: Well, that was that was the topic that I absolutely did not want to discuss. I never asked him about this. I only know that he did manage to cross over. And because whenever there is talk about this, I get really upset and agitated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, tell me, please, were you ever at that time or at any time a member of the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: Yes, until the demilitarisation I worked in the medical service. I would stoke the fire or serve as a servant. That's what I did in my village.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, tell me, do you know when the demilitarisation of Srebrenica came about and whether it -- it was fully carried out?

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't know the date. You probably are in a better position to know that, but I don't, and I don't even know how it was carried out. I just know that people who had weapons had to hand them over, and that's about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. May I remind you, this was in 1993. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: Well, I would agree with whatever anyone says about when this happened, because I don't really know exactly when it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that at this time some people surrendered their weapons while others did not? Is that how it was?

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm asking this because you testified about this in the Popovic case on page 1735. However, it's not very relevant to what we're discussing here. In your statement you said that you received humanitarian aid, you and your family. Could you just tell me how this was organised, this humanitarian aid distribution?

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: Well, how? As soon as humanitarian aid arrived, it would be distributed to the people there according to the number of family members. So we would distribute it equally for every person.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you just tell me who did this, who distributed the aid?

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: Well, it was done in villages. We would select one of us to actually distribute the aid, but it would be done in one of the villages. Sometimes in each village, sometimes one. There would be a post for one -- in one village for two.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you just tell us here, please, whether there was civilian protection in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you receive any information at any point that there were negotiations between the civilians and General Mladic on your transport to Tuzla on the night between the 11th and the 12th?

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: No, I didn't know of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could you tell me, please -- what you said in your statement slightly differs from what you just told us here now. It doesn't really matter much, but I want to correct this in the transcript. You said in your statement that your son, as he was going together with you, decided to split and join the column that was trying to breakthrough.

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember that I said that, but I know that he wasn't with me because I didn't find him. He wasn't at home, and I don't know what happened with him. Now, if somebody did say that or write that down, it's not really so important.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, this was in the statement that we just saw a minute ago, 1D41, on page 2 in line 10 it says: "I went with my family, my wife, and my two children. My son was 30, and my daughter 19." Have I quoted this correctly?

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: Well, I don't really know. If I mention -- if that's what I said, that's okay, but if not, I don't really know how old my children were at the time. But it's possible that I did say that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The microphone is off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, your microphone was off. Please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you. I've just been told by my legal advisor that I should repeat my question, so I'm repeating it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, is it correct that your son went with a group of able-bodied men who were attempting a breakthrough from Srebrenica to Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what I asked him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The microphone is off again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please repeat your question. Your microphone was off again.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, for your suggestion. And I also thank the witness, because he answered with a yes to my question. So his other -- his son went together with the column of able-bodied men who were trying to breakthrough to Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Correct?

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you understand me now, Mr. President? Mr. Vanderpuye, did you want to say something?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I was only indicating for you turn your microphone on. This seems to be a problem. So if you keep it on, we can probably avoid having to stop.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Vanderpuye. I will bear that in mind, and I will try to keep my microphone on or off as required.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Witness, you were telling us just a moment ago about how it was that you were taken to the school gym, and describing the pictures that the Prosecutor showed you. You said that there were about 2.000 people who were taken there. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: Well, about 2.500 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: That is your assessment, but you never actually counted those people.

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: Well, no, we didn't count them, but we just made an assessment. We -- an estimate. We just sort of tried to figure out how many people were sitting around us, and on the basis of that we would make an estimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: But in what gym was it and how large was it? Could you tell us?

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: Well, I can't tell you how big the gym was, but if I were -- if you were to ask me, I could confirm it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, you said it was -- in your statement that it was 15 by 20 metres long. Is that how it was?

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: Well, I can't tell you now, but if that's what I said then, then that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, do you believe that so many people can actually fit into a room that big?

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: Well, if somebody was shooting above your head and was standing in front of you, you would try and push back as far as you could, and we did that. We pushed against each other. We were -- we were as close as sardines in a can, and some people even suffocated because of that, how tightly packed we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, thank you, Witness. If I were in that position, I -- I didn't mean to question anything that you said before. I was just putting questions to you.

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: Well, just go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Witness, you stated here that on several occasions, and looking at your statement I realise that that was on six occasions, you said that you saw General Mladic and that you saw him on the 14th of July.

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: That's correct. I saw him on six occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Well, do you still claim that you saw him on the 14th of July as well, that you saw him on several occasions on site? Could you just tell us about what time was it that you saw him?

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: Well, I saw him outside the gym, perhaps I think around midday, but I can't really say for sure; whereas at the site where we were executed, it was perhaps an hour before dark.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could you tell us then approximately how late could that have been?

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: Well, I think perhaps around 7.00, maybe a little after 7.00. He arrived in a red car. This car was following the TAM truck and go back with the truck, and on this occasion he -- the car parked. He got out, and the man who was sitting next to the driver as well. The driver had a grey -- olive-grey uniform; whereas Mladic had a camouflage uniform on. They stood there and waited till everyone was shot dead, and then when that was done, they went back into the car and drove off the same -- in the same direction from which they had come.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you tell us at about what time this was?

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: This was about 7.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, could you tell us, was this vehicle -- did you see it in Srebrenica? Was it close to the truck?

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: Well, the same exact type of vehicle followed us -- or, rather, went before our bus and took us to the Bratunac warehouse. As from our trip from Bratunac, I didn't see any others. I saw another bus in front us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You've answered my question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, before this session, Mr. McCloskey gave a statement to my legal advisors and to me which we weren't able to see before because this witness was scheduled quite -- was actually inserted not according to the schedule to testify today. So I would appreciate if the Prosecutor could pull up this statement which was taken on the 6th of June, 2006, by an UNPROFOR person.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter is -- could the witness please -- could the accused please repeat the date of this statement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please repeat the date of this statement.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The statement was taken on the 6th of June, 2000, and it is a statement about the 14th of July of 1995, the day that the witness and I were discussing in my last questions put to him. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, and thank you to my colleague. It was I who provided the statement to Mr. Gajic this morning. This is a document that was previously disclosed on 7 March 2008. It was loaded into e-court under 6201. So if Mr. Tolimir would like to access it, that's what it is. But I just want the record to be clear that there's a document notwithstanding the scheduling of the witness that was available to the Defence more than a year ago, or almost two years ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, do you want to have that up on the screen?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Yes, I would like it on the screen so that the Trial Chamber could also see it, because in it the events that I discuss with the witness are described, and this was provided by Major Elliot from UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We should wait for -- with your next question until the moment we have it on the screen. It's only in English in e-court. There's no translation yet. I suggest that Mr. Vanderpuye and Mr. Gajic could clarify this situation, and we have our break now.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I'm not sure exactly what the issue is. I provided the document to Mr. Gajic this morning because I told Mr. Gajic depending on the direction of the cross-examination, it might be a document that I might need to use in redirect examination. These are both documents that were disclosed to the Defence years ago. So if the Defence intended to use it on cross-examination, certainly had ample notice and opportunity to do so. So maybe that's what the issue is, and maybe that's what's a bit confusing. It's very clear, I think, that the Defence has the document and can use it anyway they wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you have the statement that can perhaps clarify that. I suggest that we have now our first break, and then we continue at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I don't object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We adjourn now and resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before you continue, Mr. Vanderpuye, the Registrar shall indicate a correction of a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Exhibit P59 is the unredacted version of the transcript and not the redacted as previously stated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, and good afternoon to you and -- good morning still to you and Your Honours, good afternoon, Judge Mindua. I've spoken -- I've had an opportunity to speak to Mr. Gajic, and I think we've resolved -- I think we've resolved the issue with respect to the document in question, so I just wanted to alert you to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir, you may continue your examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I wish to greet once again everyone who is present or who is following this, and I wish that they have the peace of God with them. I wanted to thank the Prosecutor for alerting us at this stage about this document, because this witness talks about the events of the 14th that we recently discussed. My legal assistants have this document, and they did not intend to propose it at this stage. However, I did. I decided to tender it now because the date is characteristic and so is the testimony of this gentleman, both the general and both this witness, and if you would allow me, I would ask this witness a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Do you want to have this document on the screen?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We could see the document. It's 65 ter 503.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Perhaps we wait a moment until we have it on the screen. It's -- oh, it's also in B/C/S. Carry on, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, I would ask you how you measured the time during the day and night and during day time?

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: I had a watch, so that's how I measured it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you also have dates on your watch?

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: On the basis of what did you determine the date?

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: I knew when I left and then when night would fall and when the next day would come, and so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it possible that you have mixed the day of the 14th with another day?

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: What did I say about the 14th that happened then?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You said that the execution at the location where you were was finished on the 14th, and that in the night between the 14th and the 15th you began to withdraw towards Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: It's possible that I made a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: If you made a mistake, was that on the 13th or a day later?

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: On the 11th in the evening we came to Potocari. On the 12th we got to Bratunac. On the 13th and on the 14th the execution took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So on the 15th you were already moving in the direction of Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. I would read something to you, and you can tell us whether this was possible. I don't even have to read it out. It's enough for me to say that. There is a witness here who says that at the time that you talked about, that they were with General Mladic all the time. This general says that he was with Ratko Mladic all the time at a meeting between 1900 until 2200 hours on the 14th of July, 1995, in Belgrade. Is it possible that General Mladic could be in two places, where you said he was and where this general says he was?

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: And what was the time when he was there?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: From 1700 hours onwards.

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: From 17 hours, 1700 hours? It's not possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: He says 1900 hours.

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: He says 1900 hours. 7.00 p.m. he was where we were at the shooting site about 7.00 p.m. But it's possible that around 8.00 p.m. that he flew away and that he was there then. But around 7.00 p.m., he was right where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: All right. If the President will allow me, I can read out the sentence to you.

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: Yes, you can read it out, but I have heard it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I read it out? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, the Presiding Judge allows me. Here I will read it for you: "Later that same evening at approximately 1900 hours, Mr. Bildt and General de Lapresle met with President Milosevic and General Ratko Mladic, commander of the Main Staff of the Bosnian Serb army. This meeting concluded at approximately 2200 hours on the 14th of July, 1995."

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: On the 14th?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I've been warned to wait until the interpreter interprets it. I will tell you that the general says it was on the 14th of July, 1995, from 1900 hours until 2200 hours in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: It could not have been from 1900 hours, but around 2000 hours he could have flown there in a helicopter to say what sort of crime he had committed and to give a report about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you about your answer. For your information only, I can tell you that on the 15th of July, in case you mixed the dates, if you remember later on tell us: "On the 15th of July in Belgrade the same general attended a meeting with President Milosevic and other members of his delegation in Belgrade and General Ratko Mladic was also present. The meeting began at around 1200 hours and concluded at about 2200 hundred hours. During this time General Mladic remained in my presence."

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: From the 14th at 7.00 p.m. I have no idea where Mladic was. I did not know, and he could have been anywhere. I wouldn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. I just wanted in good faith to ask you this and see if you had made a mistake. This is why I ask you how you measured time, but you told me you had a watch.

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now ask you another question. When you left in the direction of Tuzla from the execution site on the 14th, did you come across the Serbian Army? Where and where when? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: Maybe on the fourth day I came across an ambush close to where the lines were. That was in the evening, and I couldn't pass through because they shot at us, so I couldn't pass through and we went back, and that was where we spent the day. In the next evening we were walking along a brook between the two positions, and going down along the brook we came to our territory maybe at about 2.00 a.m. I do not know that for certain, but it was after midnight.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did they fire on you at the time, or were the soldiers sleeping next to whose positions you passed?

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: No, but we heard shots in the forest and some twigs were broken. So in the morning we could see that we had been close to them. They just felt our presence and they started shooting again.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Will you tell me whether when you came here this time, did you come together with some other witnesses who came to testify here in The Hague, or did you travel here alone?

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: I was alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And wherever you are staying here, did you have any contact with any other persons from the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: I didn't see anyone, nor did I get in touch with anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. While you travelled from the place where you were on the 14th to Tuzla, did you talk about the events with other persons that you were going with? I won't mention their names because many of them are protected witnesses.

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: There was not much to talk about. We were just discussing how we could cross, where we should go, and we tried to reach an agreement about that, but we had survived the same thing so there was not much to discuss.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Can you tell me if you are returning to Bosnia-Herzegovina now, or if you are returning to another location where you live? I won't mention it unless you want me to.

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: I think that you don't need to know that particularly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You are right. I won't say that. I'm just asking whether you're returning to Bosnia-Herzegovina or to another location where you are living, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: Where -- I'll go wherever I wish to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: All right. I wish to thank you. I wish you a safe trip back. Thanks for your answers. Thanks for your testimony. I have no other questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PW-023
utterances.text: Thank you as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Tolimir. Mr. Vanderpuye, do you have re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, I do not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sir, that concludes the questioning, the examination for you. You will be pleased to know --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You will be pleased to know that you may now return to your normal activities. The Chamber and I think everybody in the courtroom would like to thank you that you was able -- were able to come again to The Hague and to tell us what you were -- had to go through during these days. Thank you very much again, and the court officer will assist you to leave the courtroom. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too, Your Honours, and to all the personnel who welcomed me heartily here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Good-bye, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me. I just wanted to say as I was reading a part of this document, if you allow, I would tender it into evidence. If not, we would do that later because we have it now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you like to deal with this document as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: We have no objection if he would like to tender that into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit D3, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I just wanted to ask if I may be excused at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Of course, but I think we adjourn now because there is no other witness available as I --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think there is an issue that one of my colleagues would like to address with respect to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Vanderpuye. Mr. McCloskey -- Mr. Thayer. Good morning and welcome, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good morning Mr. President, Your Honours. Good morning, General Tolimir, Mr. Gajic. Good morning everyone. Thanks to Dutch medical care, Mr. Oric is well enough to begin his testimony today. He's not a hundred per cent, but he is willing -- willing to start. Unfortunately, I didn't know that in time to be able to advise Mr. Gajic that he would be testifying today. As of Friday I thought there would be no chance, frankly, that he would be available this week. But he is well enough. We would like to, at the very least, conclude his direct testimony today and then pick up with his cross-examination on Thursday. I don't anticipate it will be more than half an hour or so total for his direct testimony, but at least we can complete that today. We do have another witness available in addition to the Skorpions video which is about 20 minutes of a video-tape to play that our friends have been notified about for some time now. So we do have this investigator to testify briefly about a map book that we have advised our friends about. It's a simple book of maps that we have used, relied upon. We have provided translations of the pertinent parts of those maps. We have an investigator who is prepared to testify very briefly about the underlying materials in support of each map. Not going into detail about the locations and distances and the meaning of these locations for the purposes of the case, but to give the Trial Chamber an idea of how we came across these maps and what they consist of, what the bases of the maps are, and again that would be about half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Did I understand you correctly that we now start with the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We are prepared to do that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Then the Chamber appreciates that, that we don't lose court time.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Then the next witness could be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Oric.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The Chamber is happy that your health is better again now, and welcome to the Tribunal. Could you please read aloud the affirmation on the card which is shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And now please sit down. Mr. Thayer for the Prosecution has some questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Would you please state your name for the record.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC
utterances.text: Mevludin Oric.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, I understand you're still not feeling a hundred per cent. If you need to take a break at any time, please just let us know.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC
utterances.text: I will. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And please try to leave a pause between General Tolimir's questions, especially on cross-examination, also when I ask you a question, but it particularly on cross-examination since you and General Tolimir speak the same language. We don't want to have an overlapping and an overheated translation booth, okay?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC
utterances.text: All right. I'm familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, do you recall testifying over a period of four days in August of 2006 in another case?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did you listen to that testimony over a couple of days last week?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And was that testimony accurately recorded?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, sir, if you were asked the same questions today in this courtroom that you were asked back in August of 2006, would your answers be the same?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC
utterances.text: Yes. They're always the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, at this time the Prosecution would offer 65 ter 6194 and 6195, the redacted and public versions of the witness's prior testimony respectively.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: They will be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: At this time we would --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P68 under seal for the under seal transcript of the testimony, and P69 for the redacted public version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: At this time, Mr. President, we would also tender the following exhibits that were part of the witness's prior testimony. Those are 65 ter numbers 1441, 1442, 3326, 3327, 3328, and 3329.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. They will be received and given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. 65 ter 1441 will be Exhibit P70. 65 ter 1442 will be Exhibit P71. 65 ter 3326 will be Exhibit P72. 65 ter 3327 will be Exhibit P73. 65 ter 3328 will be Exhibit P74. 65 ter 3329 will be Exhibit P75.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: With the Court's permission, I'll read the 92 ter summary that I've prepared. During the war, the witness served as the commander of a ten-man manoeuvre squad manning the lines in the area near his village between UNPROFOR check-points. They would man the lines and then return home and work their land, then return to the line. He wore civilian clothes throughout the war and did not have a uniform. In July 1995, there were approximately 14.000 able-bodied men in Srebrenica, most of whom were not armed. The witness was in his sister's house in Srebrenica when the shelling began in the first week of July. The town was full of civilians and everything was targeted, so shells fell wherever they could fall. He estimates that shelling continued day and night for approximately seven days. The witness was part of the approximately 15.000-person column which left on foot for Tuzla. The column was ambushed along the way, including his portion of the column, which was ambushed in the evening of 12 July in the forest near Kamenica, Bratunac municipality, as it headed toward Konjevic Polje. The witness spent the whole day of 13 July in the area of Konjevic Polje with the Bratunac-Konjevic Polje road to his right. In the evening of 13 July, he and eight others headed towards the Bratunac-Konjevic Polje road where they were captured by Serb forces and taken to a warehouse in Konjevic Polje. Two buses arrived later that night and transported his group to Bratunac. In Bratunac, the witness's bus parked in a column of buses in front of the entrance to the Vuk Karadzic school and spent the night there. During the night of 13 July, prisoners were taken from his bus and other buses and never returned. He heard screaming, moaning, and bursts of gunfire coming from the school throughout the night, and during the night the prisoners were given water but no food. In the morning of 14 July, the prisoners in the buses were taken to Zvornik in a convoy of buses and trucks led by an UNPROFOR APC manned by Serb soldiers. The convoy and APC stopped at a school where the prisoners were ordered to run from the buses across a concrete football pitch into the school. There were soldiers guarding both sides of the football pitch as the prisoners ran into the gym, and the prisoners were ordered to leave their belongings in a pile in front of the school before entering. The prisoners entered the gym where they were ordered to sit with their knees under their chins or be shot. Temperature was terrible in the gym, and it was difficult to breathe in the position in which they had been ordered to sit, and prisoners, especially the elderly, began fainting, but were so tightly packed that they could not fall over. There were three or four boys among the prisoners who were told to fetch water, but it did not reach beyond the middle of the gym where the witness was. During the time he was in the gym, the prisoners were given no food or medical attention. In the afternoon of 14 July, the prisoners were ordered out of the gym in groups, blindfolded, given some water, and ordered onto trucks. Somewhere between 1300 to 1500 hours, the witness stepped into the back of one of the trucks and sat on a bench, followed by some of his relatives, including his cousin, Haris Hasanovic. After four or five minutes the driving the trucks pulled over and the prisoners were ordered to hurry up and jump out onto a meadow. The witness held hands with his cousin who told him, "They are going to kill us," and as soon as the witness replied, "No, they're not," the shooting started. His cousin was shot and fell on top the witness who pretended to be dead as his cousin died on top of him. As the witness lay amid the dead, every four or five minutes he heard more trucks arrive and prisoners ordered to line up followed by bursts of gunfire. This pattern continued throughout the night and wounded prisoners were executed with single gunshots. The witness also heard the engine sounds of heavy machinery operating nearby. The witness fainted or fell asleep and woke during the night to see that the area was lit up by the lights of an excavator while the shooting continued. At one point the shooting stopped, and he heard someone say that they had finished. He heard the engines turn off and the people leave. The witness waited 10 or 15 minutes after the people left and tried to move his body, which was numb and still under his cousin's body. When he was finally able to stand up, there was moonlight, and he saw the meadow filled with corpses. He was very afraid and began to cry, and he heard someone ask if he was wounded, and he headed towards the voice. He met up with another survivor, and as the witness and that other survivor fled the meadow sometime past midnight, they saw a deep grave dug by an excavator which was parked next to the grave along with a front-end loader. The next day the witness and the other survivor encountered a third survivor, Smajil Hodzic. The three men made it to Nezuk on the 21st of July. If I may, Mr. President, I have just a few follow-up questions for the witness. May we have 65 ter 1442 on e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And while we're waiting for that to come up, sir, I just want to let you know we're going to spend a couple of moments looking at a sketch which you testified about in 2006, and I won't ask you any particulars about the features on that sketch because that's all in your prior testimony and the Trial Chamber has that, so we don't need to go over it, but I just want to clarify one or two matters about the sketch. Do you see the sketch in front you, sir?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, this is how it appeared in e-court in the prior case, and as we can see, it appears to be more or less a black-and-white scan of your sketch. Now, last week you and I had an opportunity to look at the original sketch that you drew, the original of what we are seeing on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And with the usher's assistance -- Madam Usher. I'm not sure who it is today. I would like to put the original on the ELMO and look at it the old-fashioned way, because I think we need to look at the original for the one or two questions I have. I have it here. I've shown the original to my friends on the other side, so they've had an opportunity to look at this. Now, we have the original here on the ELMO --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: It's a little easier to see, but should the Court wish, I can hand up the original to the Trial Chamber for its inspection.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: But, sir, can you tell us on this sketch whether you see some handwriting in black ink and some handwriting in blue ink.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber whose handwriting is in the black ink, first of all.

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC
utterances.text: The black ink is what I wrote down, whereas the investigators used the blue-ink pen and wrote down in their own language, but I wrote in black ink and explained what was what, and as the interpreters interpreted, they would jot it down in blue ink. So the blue ink is the investigator's ink, and black is mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And just one quick follow-up question, sir. I take it -- or can you tell us, was that at the same time? In other words, was the English translation, as it were, in blue ink done in your presence or not?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was done in my presence.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I think we're done with that exhibit. Thank you, Madam Usher. And, Your Honours, I can -- Mr. President, I can hand this up to the Court for the Court's review just to -- it's still hard to see on the ELMO to see the difference, but I think it's fair to say you can see the difference when it's up close, and I will not be offering this as a new exhibit because I think we'll just get the same scan into e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, in your testimony in -- in another case, you mentioned that the warehouse in Konjevic Polje in which you were held before being taken to Bratunac no longer exists today. Can you tell the Trial Chamber what replaced that warehouse in Konjevic Polje?

utterances.speaker: MEVLUDIN ORIC
utterances.text: Well, today there's a gas station in the place where the warehouses used to be, so the warehouses were torn down, pulled down, and a gas station was built, and that's where it is today.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You testified in the last trial that you and the other survivor, and I won't give his name here, but you and another survivor met up with a third survivor named Smajil Hodzic as you were trying to make it to free territory. Do you recall that, sir?
